title: AI receptionist vs human receptionist: Compared
summary: Two ways to answer your business calls, and they cost vastly different amounts. Here is what each actually does well, and where AI genuinely falls short.
body_markdown:
Your business phone rings at 8 p.m. on a Tuesday. No one is available to take the call. The caller hangs up and tries your competitor instead.


Missed calls are usually what push a small business toward a receptionist. You have options: an AI receptionist or a human receptionist. Both handle your incoming calls, but they work differently. A virtual receptionist is a real person, while an AI receptionist is software that interacts with your customers.


In addition to the cost comparison of an AI receptionist vs a human receptionist, we’ll cover the benefits and trade-offs.


##


What are the options for a receptionist?


Small businesses have several receptionist options.


### 1. AI receptionist


An AI receptionist is software that can answer calls 24/7. It uses natural language processing, or NLP, to understand callers. Based on what the caller needs, it can take actions such as booking an appointment, sending a text message, or routing the call.


You’re billed by usage tiers that bundle a set number of calls or minutes.


### 2. Virtual receptionist


A[virtual receptionist](https://www.quo.com/blog/what-is-a-virtual-receptionist/) service uses a real person working remotely to handle calls. These are also sometimes called live answering services. Operators follow a script and handle multiple clients or businesses.


You’re billed monthly, per call, or per minute. Virtual receptionists usually provide coverage during regular business hours unless you pay extra.


### 3. In-house receptionist


An in-house receptionist is your employee. An in-person receptionist may sit in your office, greeting customers and answering the phone. Or the receptionist might answer calls remotely. Whether part-time or full-time, you’re paying a[salary](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/office-and-administrative-support/receptionists.htm) , plus benefits and payroll taxes.


##


What you’ll pay for an AI vs human receptionist


Monthly cost is where these options differ the most. Here’s a breakdown of what you can expect:


Option Cost structure Typical price range Pricing factors


AI receptionist Usage tiers that bundle a set number of calls or minutes $25–$300+ per month Call volume, overages, additional languages, available features


Virtual receptionist/live answering service Monthly retainer that bundles a set number of calls or minutes $300–$2,500+ per month Call volume, overages, after-hours coverage, rounding increments


In-house receptionist Salary plus benefits and payroll taxes ~[$34,000–$48,000](https://www.salary.com/research/salary/benchmark/receptionist-i-salary) per year Location, hours, seniority


AI receptionist costs start low.


- **Quo** lets you make your first 10 calls with our AI voice agent[Sona](https://www.quo.com/sona) for free, so you can test it out. After that, $25 per month covers about 40 calls.
- [Smith.ai](https://www.quo.com/blog/smith-ai-alternatives/) provides AI virtual receptionist services starting at $150 per month for around 75 calls or human-first answering for $300 per month for 30 calls.
- **Go Answer** charges $175 per month for 100 minutes of live answering or $95 per month for 100 minutes of AI receptionist time.


When you’re buying a package of minutes for a service, consider the length of your average call. For example, 100 minutes could be between 20 and 30 calls. Live answering services may ‌round up their minutes. A three-minute phone call might be charged to your account as five minutes, depending on rounding.


Read the fine print before you commit. Check what counts as a billable call and how much each overage minute or call costs. Quo doesn’t count calls under 15 seconds, but some providers would still charge for the time spent picking up the phone. The complaint we hear most often about human services is not sticker shock on its own. It’s paying a premium rate and still having to check the work.


For a deeper look at pricing, see our guides on[virtual receptionist cost](https://www.quo.com/blog/virtual-receptionist-cost/) and[answering service cost](https://www.quo.com/blog/answering-service-cost/) .


##


How each receptionist option helps your business


Artificial intelligence handles call volume without wait times and is great for routine calls. A live answering service is better for complex calls, like billing or service issues. Here’s a breakdown:


AI receptionist Virtual receptionist/live answering service


**Response times** Instant Depends on the queue


**Availability** 24/7 Business hours unless you pay more


**Consistency** Identical on every call Script-led, varies by operator


**Knows your business** Depends on your knowledge base Learns over time


**Multilingual support** Available, depends on provider Varies, depends on services offered


**Simultaneous calls** Can handle simultaneous inbound calls Can't handle without additional staff


**Scalability** Handles any call volume Requires hiring more staff


**Best at** Overflow, after-hours, appointment scheduling, call routing High-value and sensitive calls


**Reaches a caller who did not stay on the line** Yes.[Replies by text to a missed call](https://www.quo.com/sona#leads-over-sms) , or to someone who texted instead of calling No. The contact never reaches the service


##


Where an AI receptionist falls short


Many callers figure out they’re talking to AI within seconds. They may not mind, as long as their issue is resolved quickly. But in some situations, a human receptionist provides a better customer experience.


- **Emotional calls.** Someone calling while upset wants human empathy. AI can be polite, but it can frustrate a caller who wants to talk to a person.
- **Judgment calls.** A receptionist who’s been at your company for two years knows your clients. AI follows rules and can’t pick up on client preferences.
- **Unscripted situations.** A person improvises, but AI escalates to a human. Escalation is the safe move, but someone has to be available on the other end.
- **Anything outside the knowledge base.** AI can’t answer what it was never told. You need to spend some time setting up an AI receptionist for it to perform well.


A human receptionist’s biggest limitation is availability. Sick days, vacation days, after-hours calls, and even time zones impact a human’s ability to answer the phone. If your biggest goal is to have every call answered, you’ll still have gaps with a human receptionist.


##


How AI solves the after-hours coverage gap


After-hours coverage is often where small businesses are hit the hardest. You’re not available, *and* a virtual receptionist isn’t available — yet it’s a call you don’t want to miss. Some virtual receptionist providers offer extended-hours coverage for an additional fee, but you’d need to decide whether the cost is worth it.


An AI receptionist can detect urgency and use call forwarding to transfer the call to an emergency number. As a[missed call service](https://www.quo.com/features/missed-call-service) , Sona catches every call so no one goes to voicemail.


##


The hybrid setup that works for most businesses


Many businesses end up with a hybrid model of a human and a virtual receptionist.


An AI receptionist covers call overflow and after-hours calls. It captures leads and qualifies them, syncing the details to your CRM. A person takes the calls that need judgment. In both instances, urgent calls are routed to whoever is on call.


Here’s how ER Fukuda, the CEO and Co-Founder of Rainbow Road Transport, uses a hybrid approach:


*“We used Quo for incoming calls, with live agents answering calls directly. This worked well during business hours, but we struggled to manage the overflow. Sona has been instrumental in filling those gaps. It collects key information from the caller, so when our agents return in the morning, they have a queue of qualified leads to process, which speeds up our response time and improves booking conversion.”*


This setup keeps costs down without leaving any gaps in call coverage.


##


The verdict


For most small businesses, AI is the clear choice for routine calls. At $25 per month versus hundreds for a live service, the math is straightforward.

##


FAQs


**Is an AI receptionist better than a human receptionist?**


For routine calls and repeat questions, AI answers faster and costs a fraction as much. For emotional or high-value calls, a person is the better choice. Many businesses use both rather than choosing one. Compare your options in our[best AI receptionist](https://www.quo.com/blog/best-ai-phone-answering-services/) round-up.


**Will an AI receptionist replace my receptionist?**


Usually not. Many businesses keep their receptionists and use AI for overflow and after-hours coverage. If your receptionist answers the same five questions all day, AI can take that repetitive work off their plate.


**What’s the difference between an AI receptionist and a virtual receptionist?**


A virtual receptionist is a live person who answers calls on your behalf. An AI receptionist is software that handles calls automatically. Marketing teams often use the terms interchangeably. Watch for this when comparing prices — AI receptionists should be significantly cheaper since there’s no actual person on the line.


**Do callers mind talking to an AI receptionist?**


Many callers figure out fairly fast that they’re talking to software. The research on preferences is mixed. What comes through consistently is that people don’t like waiting or repeating themselves.[A fast, accurate AI often gets a better reaction](https://www.parloa.com/blog/cx-automation-has-a-trust-problem/#:~:text=84.9%25%20of%20customers%20say%20they%27d%20keep%20using%20automated%20systems%20if%20those%20systems%20resolved%20their%20issues%20consistently.) than a slow hold queue
